rows.label: Concept
rows.text: All three equations of motion follow from the straight-line $v$–$t$ graph of uniform acceleration: the slope gives $v = u + at$; the area (rectangle + triangle, or the trapezoid mean-height $\frac{u+v}{2}t$) gives $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$; eliminating $t$ yields $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$. The $a$–$t$ graph (area = change in velocity) and the $x$–$t$ parabola complete the graphical picture.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$v = u + at$ (slope of $v$–$t$ line)
$s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ (rectangle + triangle area)
$s = \left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right)t$ (trapezoid mean-height form)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Constant Acceleration Requirement:** The three equations $v = u + at$, $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ are valid *only* when acceleration is constant. If $a$ varies with time, position, or velocity, these algebraic equations fail — one must use the graphical area method or calculus ($v = \int a dt$, $s = \int v dt$).  ·  **Graphical Derivation Logic:** The $v$-$t$ graph for constant $a$ is a straight line. Slope = $a$ gives $v = u + at$. Area (trapezoid) = $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$. Eliminating $t$ gives $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$. These derivations are NEB favorites.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: Always draw and label the $v$–$t$ graph in derivation questions — the diagram itself carries marks.  ·  Note 2: For two-stage journeys (accelerate then brake), apply the equations to EACH stage and add the areas.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Example 1 (slope): a cyclist's $v$–$t$ line rises from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s → $a = \frac{10-2}{4} = 2$ m/s², read straight off the graph.  ·  Example 2 (area): the same cyclist covers $s = \frac{2+10}{2} \times 4 = 24$ m — the trapezoid area, no equation needed.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'The area under the $v$–$t$ graph gives acceleration.' ✅ Area gives DISPLACEMENT; the SLOPE gives acceleration. Swap-proof: slope of $v$–$t$ = $a$ (m/s²), area of $v$–$t$ = $s$ (m).  ·  ❌ Using $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ for the distance in the $n$-th second directly with $t = n$. ✅ That gives the total distance in $n$ seconds. The $n$-th SECOND distance is $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$, i.e. $s(n) - s(n-1)$.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Perform all three graphical derivations with a single labelled figure, from memory.  ·  Task 2: Solve ten numericals classifying them by which equation fits (u/v/a/t/s given-asked table).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Given/asked table — list u, v, a, t, s; the equation missing BOTH the unknown and the unwanted quantity is your equation.  ·  Trick 2: Braking distance without time: $s = u^2/2|a|$ — memorise this special case of the third equation.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Derive the three equations of motion using a velocity–time graph (label the initial velocity, final velocity, time and area regions).  ·  Q2. Show that the area under the $v$–$t$ graph equals $ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ for uniformly accelerated motion.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 1: The graphical derivation of $v = u + at$ and $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ is a repeating NEB theory question — practise the labelled figure.  ·  Exam Tip 2: In numericals, write the chosen equation first, then substitute — method marks live in the equation selection.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Concept 1: Graphical derivation — slope gives $v = u + at$; area gives $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.  ·  Concept 2: Eliminating $t$ between equations yields the time-free form $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.  ·  Concept 3: Average-velocity form $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t$ as the trapezoid mean height.  ·  Concept 4: $n$-th second distance $s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1)$ and the odd-number pattern.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Slope of $v$–$t$ = acceleration; area under $v$–$t$ = displacement.  ·  The three equations hold ONLY for constant acceleration.  ·  $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ is the equation of choice when time is unknown.  ·  $s = \left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right)t$ is the graphical 'average velocity × time' form.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The velocity–time 'trapezoid' derivation appears in Galileo's reasoning (via inclined planes and odd-number distances) two centuries before formal calculus existed.  ·  Air-force and driving-school 'stopping distance' charts are exactly the $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ equation with $v = 0$ — doubling speed quadruples braking distance.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. A bus moving at 60 km/h decelerates uniformly at 2 m/s². Find the time and distance to stop.  ·  Q4. Derive the distance covered in the $n$-th second, $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$, using two areas.  ·  Q5. State the condition of validity of the equations of motion and what replaces them when the condition fails.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 3: Convert all units to SI (km/h ÷ 3.6) before any substitution, and state the sign convention used.  ·  Exam Tip 4: Multi-stage questions (lift, train, rocket) reward a quick $v$–$t$ sketch before any algebra.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Example 3 (third equation): a car at 25 m/s needs to stop within 50 m. Required deceleration: $0 = 25^2 + 2a(50) \Rightarrow a = -6.25$ m/s² — time never enters, which is why this equation fits.  ·  Example 4 (two-stage motion): a train accelerates at 1 m/s² for 20 s then brakes at 2 m/s² to stop. Draw the $v$–$t$ trapezoid; peak speed 20 m/s; total distance = area = 300 m.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version derives all three equations of motion graphically (from the velocity–time graph) — the derivation style NEB asks for 'using a graphical method'.  ·  **Setup:** a body starts with initial velocity $u$ and accelerates uniformly at $a$; after time $t$ its velocity is $v$. On a $v$–$t$ graph this is a straight line from $(0, u)$ to $(t, v)$ — the straightness is exactly the meaning of uniform acceleration.  ·  **First equation (from the slope):** slope of the line = acceleration $a = \frac{v - u}{t}$. Rearranging: $v = u + at$ — 'final velocity = initial velocity + rate of change of velocity × time'.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Validity condition — constant acceleration; otherwise graphical areas or calculus.  ·  $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ (time eliminated)  ·  $s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$ (distance in the $n$-th second)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Sign Convention Consistency:** Choose one positive direction (e.g., up = +) and keep it. For free fall, $a = -g$ if up is +. For braking, $a$ is opposite to $v$. The equations work with signed quantities; plug in signs consistently.  ·  Sign convention decides deceleration: keep one positive direction throughout the problem.  ·  Distance in the $n$-th second ≠ distance in $n$ seconds — the classic NEB distinction.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Applying $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with sign errors during braking. ✅ Take one positive direction and keep it: braking at 20 m/s with $a = -5$ m/s² gives $0 = 400 + 2(-5)s \Rightarrow s = 40$ m — the minus sign is essential.  ·  ❌ 'The equations work if acceleration changes gradually.' ✅ All three equations REQUIRE constant acceleration; if $a$ varies, use graphs/areas or calculus.  ·  ❌ Treating $u$ and $v$ as interchangeable. ✅ $u$ is the velocity at $t = 0$; $v$ is at time $t$. A body dropped from rest has $u = 0$; a body thrown up has $u = +20$ m/s while $a = -10$ m/s².

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Confusing distance with displacement when the body reverses. ✅ The equations give displacement (vector). For total path length through a reversal, split the motion at the $v = 0$ instant and add the two parts.  ·  Example 5 (drop with initial speed): a stone thrown down a well at 2 m/s strikes water 3 s later: $s = 2(3) + \tfrac{1}{2}(10)(9) = 51$ m — the rectangle-plus-triangle areas directly.  ·  Note 3: Convert km/h to m/s before substituting (divide by 3.6) — the most common numerical slip.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Note 4: If the body reverses direction, compute each leg separately and add magnitudes for distance, not displacement.  ·  Note 1: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ contains no time — use it whenever $t$ is unknown or irrelevant.  ·  Note 2: The mean-velocity form $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t$ is valid only for constant acceleration (it is the trapezoid's average height).
